props.title: The Candidate

sections.content: The Candidate stands as one of the most incisive political films ever made, with Robert Redford delivering a career-defining performance as Bill McKay, an idealistic lawyer transformed by the campaign machine. The film's documentary-style approach, influenced by director Michael Ritchie's background in television, created a template for political dramas that influenced everything from Primary Colors (1998) to Game Change (2012). What sets The Candidate apart is its unflinching look at how marketing and media manipulation shape modern politics, themes that feel even more relevant today than in 1972.

sections.content: The cynical brilliance of The Candidate lies in its prescient understanding of image-making in politics. The film's famous final line - "What do we do now?" - echoes through later works like Wag the Dog (1997) and In the Loop (2009), which similarly explore the gap between campaign promises and political reality. Cinematographer John Korty's vérité style creates an immediacy that makes viewers feel like embedded journalists, a technique later mastered in films like Good Night, and Good Luck (2005).

What distinguishes The Candidate from other political films is its focus on the gradual corruption of idealism. Unlike the outright cynicism of All the President's Men (1976) or the paranoid thriller aspects of The Manchurian Candidate (1962), this film shows how good intentions get compromised one small decision at a time. This influence can be seen in modern works like The Ides of March (2011) and Miss Sloane (2016), which similarly explore the personal cost of political ambition. sections.content: The Candidate's examination of media manipulation in politics laid groundwork for sharper satires like Network (1976) and Bob Roberts (1992). Its influence extends to contemporary works like Vice (2018) and Bombshell (2019), which similarly decode the intersection of media and political power. The film's understanding of how television shapes political narrative remains startlingly relevant in today's social media landscape.
